title: The Bohr–Bury Scheme of Electronic Configuration
notes: The Bohr–Bury scheme (1921) — the shell-filling rules that Bohr's model alone could not give. It explains how the periodic table was first built from orbits and where it needed repair (a defect of the Bohr framework).
1. **Capacity rule:** the maximum number of electrons in a shell n is 2n² — K 2, L 8, M 18, N 32.
2. **Octet rule (valence shells):** the outermost shell cannot hold more than 8 electrons; when it has 8 (noble-gas configuration: He duplet, Ne octet) the shell is stable and a new shell begins.

3. **Filling order:** shells fill roughly in order of increasing energy; within a shell, electrons enter before a new shell starts — except that 4s begins filling before 3d is complete (the (n + l) order in modern language).
• Explained chemical inertness of the noble gases (closed shells) and the valency pattern of the main groups.
• Connected atomic number with the periodic law: element 11 (Na) starts the third shell, so period 3 begins — the periodicity of properties follows from shell structure.
• Predicted the electron configurations up to about Z = 20 reliably (K, Ca).
### Where the scheme fails (defects of the Bohr framework)
• No subshell concept: it cannot explain why 4s fills before 3d, the 8/18/32 period lengths beyond period 3, or the s/p/d/f blocks.
• It ignores electron–electron repulsion and exchange energy, so anomalies like Cr ([Ar]3d⁵4s¹) and Cu ([Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹) are impossible for it.
• Orbits are still definite paths — the uncertainty principle and orbital shapes are outside the scheme; 'subshell energy order' needs penetration and shielding, i.e. the quantum-mechanical model.

The 2n² capacity survives in modern form as Σ2(2l + 1) over the subshells of shell n; the octet rule survives as the special stability of filled s + p valence sets; and the filling order is the Madelung (n + l) rule. The Bohr–Bury scheme is thus the correct skeleton with the wrong (orbital-free) flesh.
confusion: ❌ The M shell can hold 18 electrons before the N shell starts. ✅ The outermost shell is capped at 8; after 8 electrons in M, filling of N begins.
❌ The Bohr–Bury scheme is a quantum-mechanical theory. ✅ It is a shell-filling rule set from the Bohr orbit picture; subshells and orbital shapes are absent.
❌ 2n² applies to the outermost shell. ✅ 2n² is the *capacity*; the octet rule (8) restricts the valence shell's occupancy.

universalFacts: The scheme is credited to Bohr (1921) and Charles Bury (1921) independently.
It correctly predicted the closure of shells at Z = 2, 10, 18 — matching the noble gases known then.
Its failure beyond Ca (Z = 20) is the historical trigger for introducing subshells.
examples: **Problem:** Where does the Bohr–Bury scheme first fail? **Solution:** at potassium (Z = 19): the 2n²/sequence rules put the 19th electron in the M shell, but experiment and the (n + l) rule place it in 4s — the first sign that subshell energies, not shells, control filling.

summary: The Bohr–Bury scheme (1921, Bohr and Bury independently) supplied the shell-filling rules that Bohr's orbits alone could not give. Three rules: the capacity of shell n is 2n² (K 2, L 8, M 18, N 32); the outermost shell may hold at most 8 electrons, so a closed shell (He duplet or noble-gas octet) is stable and a new shell then begins; and shells fill in order of increasing energy, with electrons entering a shell before the next one starts — except that 4s begins filling before 3d is complete. The scheme explained the inertness of the noble gases, the valency pattern of the main groups, and why element 11 (Na) starts a third period, so periodicity follows from shell structure, and it gave reliable configurations up to about Z = 20. It fails beyond that because it has no subshell concept, so 4s before 3d, the 8/18/32 period lengths and the s/p/d/f blocks are outside it, and the anomalies of Cr and Cu are impossible for it.
importantConcepts: Capacity rule: shell n holds at most 2n² electrons — K 2, L 8, M 18, N 32
Octet rule: the outermost shell holds at most 8 electrons, giving duplet (He) and octet (Ne, Ar) stability
Filling order: shells fill with increasing energy, with 4s starting to fill before 3d is complete
Achievements: noble-gas inertness, main-group valency, the start of each new period, configurations up to Z ≈ 20
Defects: no subshell concept, so period lengths 8/18/32, the s/p/d/f blocks and the Cr and Cu anomalies are unexplained
importantStatements: The capacity of a shell is 2n² while the occupancy of the valence shell is limited to 8 — two different rules.
2n² is the capacity; the octet rule restricts only the outermost shell.
A closed valence shell (duplet or octet) is the shell basis of chemical inertness.
The scheme cannot express 4s filling before 3d, which first becomes obvious at potassium (Z = 19).
Electron–electron repulsion and exchange energy, which decide the real anomalies, are absent from the scheme.

keyPoints: Quote both numbers when asked: 2n² capacity, 8 maximum in the valence shell.
Shell closures at Z = 2, 10 and 18 match the noble gases known at the time.
Failure beyond calcium is the historical trigger for introducing subshells.
In modern terms the capacity becomes Σ2(2l + 1) and the order becomes the (n + l) rule.
specialNotes: The M shell can hold 18 electrons in total, but only 8 in the outermost position before N begins.
The octet rule is a statement about the valence shell only; using it for inner shells is wrong.
The scheme is a historical rule set from the orbit picture, not a quantum-mechanical theory — it contains no orbital shapes.
examShortTricks: Present the scheme as history, then contrast it with (n + l) and Hund's rule — that contrast is the mark.
K 2, L 8, M 18, N 32 should be recalled automatically.
Potassium (Z = 19) is the first element the scheme gets wrong — a reliable example.
examNotes: Stating the three rules with the capacity table is a standard 3–4 mark question.
Applications to a specific element's configuration, or to noble-gas inertness, are the usual follow-up.
One-mark items ask the maximum electrons in the outermost shell — the answer is 8.
